images.title: Why multiply by four
images.purpose: Show that 2/3 gets its own multiplier, 4, so that its bottom number also becomes 12 and both fractions count in the same unit, 1/12.
images.composition: One wide rectangular vegetable patch across the upper half, and below it two short equation cards side by side with space between them.
images.exact_structure: Top: one flat rectangular vegetable patch cut by solid vertical lines into exactly 3 equal beds. Each bed is split by thin grey #6B7280 vertical lines into 4 equal rows, making 12 equal rows. The 2 left beds, 8 rows, are filled amber #E69F00; the right bed, 4 rows, is plain. No plants drawn. Below, left: one card with the equation for 2/3, both multipliers 4 in reddish purple #CC79A7. Below, right: one card with 3/4 = 9/12 in teal #0072B2. One short line centred under the cards. Exactly 1 patch, 3 beds, 12 rows, 8 amber, 2 cards.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
beds or rows that are not all exactly equal in width
images.takeaway: Each fraction gets its own multiplier to reach 12.
images.description: A vegetable patch in 3 equal beds with 2 beds amber; each bed cut into 4 rows makes 12 rows with 8 amber, so 2/3 = 8/12, matching 3/4 = 9/12 in the same unit 1/12.
images.context: Shown with the concept as its one key picture, next to the walkthrough video. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not generated yet.
images.teaching_notes: Ask the student to point at both 12s and say why 2/3 needs 4, not 3, as its multiplier.

image_decisions.why: The patch re-cut into twelfths shows why 2/3 needs the multiplier 4; one clean picture carries it.
